candidates.topic: Honey never spoils — 3000-year-old edible honey found in Egyptian tombs
candidates.teaser: Archaeologists found something in an Egyptian tomb that was still perfectly edible after 3,000 years — and it's probably in your kitchen right now.
candidates.video_title: 3,000-Year-Old Honey Found in Egypt — Still Edible
candidates.video_description: Honey discovered in ancient Egyptian tombs was still perfectly edible after three millennia. Its unique chemistry makes it the only food that never truly expires. Find out why honey is biologically immortal.
candidates.script: Archaeologists cracking open Egyptian tombs found 3,000-year-old honey — and tasted it. It was still perfect. No mold, no bacteria, completely edible. Here's why: honey is almost entirely sugar with almost zero water. Bacteria need moisture to survive, and honey simply doesn't give them any. On top of that, honey naturally produces tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide — the same stuff used to disinfect wounds. It essentially sterilizes itself forever. As long as it stays sealed, honey has no expiration date. Literally none. So that jar sitting in your cabinet? It could outlive your great-great-grandchildren. Now the real question is — what other foods in your kitchen might actually last forever?

candidates.topic: Butterflies can remember their lives as caterpillars despite full brain dissolution
candidates.teaser: A butterfly completely dissolves its brain inside the cocoon — yet somehow still remembers things from when it was a caterpillar.
candidates.video_title: Butterflies Dissolve Their Brain — But Still Remember
candidates.video_description: Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar doesn't just transform — it completely liquefies, including its brain. Yet butterflies have been shown to retain memories from their caterpillar stage. Science still can't fully explain how.
candidates.script: Inside a cocoon, a caterpillar doesn't just grow wings. It completely dissolves into liquid — organs, muscles, and most of its brain all break down into a kind of biological soup. Scientists assumed any memories would be wiped clean. Then they ran an experiment: they trained caterpillars to avoid a specific smell using mild shocks. After full transformation, the adult butterflies still avoided that exact smell. The memories survived total liquefaction. Nobody fully understands how. Some researchers think a tiny cluster of neurons holds onto information through the entire meltdown. Which raises a deeply unsettling question — if a butterfly can remember through that, what exactly are memories made of?

candidates.topic: The Great Wall of China is not visible from space — it's a myth
candidates.teaser: One of the most repeated facts you learned in school turns out to be completely false — and NASA proved it.
candidates.video_title: You Were Lied to About the Great Wall of China
candidates.video_description: Generations of students were taught the Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye. NASA astronauts and Chinese taikonauts have confirmed this is simply not true. The myth has a surprisingly old origin.
candidates.script: You were probably taught in school that the Great Wall of China is the only man-made structure visible from space. It sounds incredible. It's also completely false. NASA confirmed it. Chinese astronaut Yang Liwei specifically looked for it during his 2003 mission — and couldn't see it. The wall is incredibly long, yes, but it's only about 5 to 8 meters wide — roughly the width of a highway lane. From space, that's invisible to the naked eye. Highways, airports, and cities are far easier to spot. The myth actually dates back to 1932 — decades before anyone had even been to space. So who decided to trust a claim nobody could verify for thirty years? And what other school facts are just as wrong?

candidates.topic: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water — the Mpemba Effect
candidates.teaser: A schoolboy in Tanzania told his teacher that hot water freezes faster than cold — and scientists have been arguing about it ever since.
candidates.video_title: Hot Water Freezes Faster Than Cold — Here's Why
candidates.video_description: The Mpemba Effect describes the counterintuitive phenomenon where hot water can freeze faster than cold water under certain conditions. Discovered by a Tanzanian student in 1963, it still divides scientists today. Physics has no clean answer.
candidates.script: In 1963, a Tanzanian schoolboy named Erasto Mpemba noticed that hot ice cream mix froze faster than cold mix. His teacher laughed at him. He wasn't wrong. He later asked a visiting physics professor to test it, and the professor was stunned — under certain conditions, hot water genuinely does freeze faster than cold water. This is now called the Mpemba Effect, and physicists have been arguing about why it happens for over sixty years. Theories include faster evaporation, dissolved gas escaping, or the way water molecules store energy. None of them fully explain every case. A kid got laughed at for noticing something real that science still can't completely explain. Makes you wonder — what else are we dismissing too quickly?

candidates.topic: The inventor of the lobotomy won a Nobel Prize
candidates.teaser: One of the most disturbing medical procedures in history didn't get its inventor fired — it got him a Nobel Prize.
candidates.video_title: The Nobel Prize Was Given for This Horrifying Surgery
candidates.video_description: António Egas Moniz invented the lobotomy — a procedure that involved severing connections in the brain's frontal lobe — and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1949. Tens of thousands of patients were lobotomized before the world realized the damage it caused.
candidates.script: In 1949, a man won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for an operation that involved drilling into someone's skull and severing parts of their brain — with no anesthesia in some cases. His name was António Egas Moniz, and the procedure was the lobotomy. At the time, it was celebrated as a breakthrough for mental illness. Tens of thousands of people — including children — were lobotomized across the world. Many were left unable to speak, feel emotions, or care for themselves. By the time doctors admitted it was causing irreversible damage, the Nobel committee refused to take the prize back. They still haven't. The Nobel Prize in Medicine was given for something now considered one of medicine's greatest ethical disasters. So what does that say about how confident we should be in today's breakthroughs?
